Combinatorics: Teaching Companion

A walkable concept map for teaching combinatorics to strong 8th-graders (AMC 10/12 flavor). Do not read it front to back like a textbook. Follow the map, teach one node at a time; each node links to a page with explanation, worked examples, figures, connections, and videos. The connections between ideas ARE the lesson, more than any single node.

🥯 Running example, the "bagel universe" (used across the simple topics instead of abstract examples): you ordered 10 bagels from Noah's Bagels in 4 types (2 Plain, 2 Sesame, 3 Everything, 3 Poppy), plus 2 spreads (plain, and onion & chives), to share among 4 kids: Varun, Kapil, Shlok, Shreyas. Different questions about these bagels introduce each idea. The capstone we build toward: in how many ways can we hand out the bagels to the 4 kids, with a spread on each? (Fully solved at Stars & Bars.)
Foundation (spine) Core technique Object / sequence Advanced technique Bridge: topic not taught here

How the four layers relate

Everything grows from a spine. Two rules do the heavy lifting: add when you choose between options, multiply when you choose in stages. Permutations are just the multiplication rule applied to arrangements, and combinations are permutations after you divide out the orderings you counted twice. That single move, correcting an overcount by dividing, is the Division Principle, and it comes back at the very top of the course in symmetry counting. So the first four chapters are not four tricks; they are one idea seen four times.

Core techniques are ways to set up a count. When the direct count is hard, you flip it (complementary counting), split it into clean cases (casework), distribute identical things (stars and bars), force a collision (pigeonhole), correct for overlap (inclusion and exclusion), match one problem onto an easier one (bijections), or express an answer in terms of smaller versions of itself (recursion). These are not new formulas; they are strategies for pointing the foundation at a messy problem. Several of them pair up: complementary counting and casework both feed inclusion and exclusion, and stars and bars, bijections, and lattice paths are really one shape shown three ways.

Objects and sequences are what those techniques keep producing. Combinations arrange themselves into Pascal's triangle, which gives the Binomial Theorem and a whole family of identities. Lattice paths turn counting into geometry and lead to the Catalan numbers. Inclusion and exclusion produces derangements; recursion produces the Fibonacci numbers; and counting divided by total possibilities gives probability, from which expected value and linearity follow. These chapters are where the techniques stop being abstract and become named results worth remembering.

Advanced techniques are power tools that unify the earlier layers. Generating functions turn a whole sequence into a single algebraic object, so recursion, the Binomial Theorem, and Fibonacci all become bookkeeping in one polynomial. Counting with symmetry (Burnside and Polya) takes the overcounting idea from chapter four and makes it exact when the overcount comes from rotations and reflections. Both chapters reach back and tie a bow on the whole map.

Where combinatorics connects outward

The pink ovals mark the frontier. This course stops there, but the ideas do not, and it helps learners to see the doors even if we do not walk through them.

Graph theory is combinatorics of dots and connections. Counting edges with the handshake idea and pushing pigeonhole into Ramsey-style guarantees both lead straight into it. Number theory shares the same tools from the other side: inclusion and exclusion gives Euler's totient, and binomial coefficients taken modulo a prime reveal deep patterns. Group theory is where symmetry counting really lives; Burnside is a first taste of orbits and group actions. And probability theory is combinatorics with the counts turned into likelihoods; our probability and expected value chapters are the on-ramp to distributions and random variables. Combinatorics is the counting layer underneath all four.

How to use this

Teach along the spine first (Counting Principles to Permutations to Combinations), then branch into techniques and objects as the map suggests. After each node, return to the map and show what it connects to, including the outward bridges. That map is the real lesson. The list below is just an index; it is not the order to teach in.

1. Counting Principles

The two rules everything is built on: multiply independent choices, add disjoint cases.

🥯 Running example, the bagel universe: you ordered 10 bagels from Noah's Bagels in 4 types: 2 Plain, 2 Sesame, 3 Everything, 3 Poppy, plus 2 spreads (plain, and onion & chives), to share among 4 kids: Varun, Kapil, Shlok, Shreyas. We'll ask questions about these bagels all the way up the map. The big one we build toward: in how many ways can we hand out the bagels (with spreads)?
Prerequisites: none. This is the root.
This node: Addition & Multiplication Principles
Unlocks: Permutations · Combinations · Stars & Bars · Inclusion-Exclusion · Probability

The core idea

Multiplication principle. If a process is a sequence of independent steps, and step \(i\) can be done in \(n_i\) ways, the whole process can be done in \[ n_1 \times n_2 \times \cdots \times n_k \text{ ways.} \] Independent means the number of options at each step doesn't depend on the earlier choices.

Addition principle. If the possibilities split into disjoint cases (no overlap), you add the counts: \[ |A \cup B| = |A| + |B| \quad\text{when } A \cap B = \varnothing. \] (When the cases can overlap, plain addition over-counts. That's exactly what Inclusion-Exclusion fixes.)

Rule of thumb the kids should chant: "AND → multiply, OR → add."

Why does multiplication work?

Think of each choice as creating a new "branch" in a tree. If you have \(n_1\) choices for step 1, you get \(n_1\) branches. At each of those branches, you have \(n_2\) choices for step 2, so each of the \(n_1\) branches splits into \(n_2\) sub-branches. That gives you \(n_1 \times n_2\) total paths. Add a third step with \(n_3\) choices? Each of the \(n_1 \times n_2\) paths splits into \(n_3\) more, giving \(n_1 \times n_2 \times n_3\) total outcomes. Multiplication counts the leaves of the tree.

Why does addition work for disjoint cases? If cases don't overlap, every outcome belongs to exactly one case. So you're just counting the union by adding up the separate piles. But if cases do overlap, you've counted the overlapping outcomes twice. That's when you need Inclusion-Exclusion to subtract the double-counted part.

Worked examples

Example 1 (multiply). A kid builds a breakfast: one of the 4 bagel types and one of the 2 spreads. How many breakfasts?

Pick a type (4 ways) and a spread (2 ways): \(4 \times 2 = 8\). The tree shows all 8.

Aha: "and" between independent choices means multiply. Each type fans out into all the spreads.

Example 2 (multiply, with a twist). We give 3 different bagel types to Varun, Kapil, and Shlok. One type each, and who gets which matters. How many ways?

Varun: any of 4 types. Kapil: any of the remaining 3. Shlok: any of the remaining 2. \[ 4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24. \]

Aha: the counts shrink because "different" removes one option each time. That falling product \(4\cdot3\cdot2\) is exactly a permutation.

Example 3 (add, then multiply). A kid wants a bagel that is either a "double" type (Plain or Sesame, the ones we have 2 of) or a "triple" type (Everything or Poppy), plus a spread. How many such breakfasts?

Type: 2 doubles or 2 triples → \(2 + 2 = 4\) type choices (disjoint, so add). Then a spread: \(\times 2\). \[ (2+2)\times 2 = 8. \]

Aha: add within a choice (disjoint alternatives), multiply across choices.

Example 4 (a bridge to the next nodes). Line up all 10 bagels in a row on the counter. Same-type bagels look identical. How many distinct line-ups?

If all 10 were distinct there'd be \(10!\) orders. But swapping the 2 identical Plain (\(2!\) ways), the 2 Sesame (\(2!\)), the 3 Everything (\(3!\)), and the 3 Poppy (\(3!\)) gives the same line-up, so we over-counted by \(2!\,2!\,3!\,3!\): \[ \frac{10!}{2!\,2!\,3!\,3!} = \frac{3{,}628{,}800}{144} = 25{,}200. \]

Aha: "count everything, then divide by what you over-counted." This move is the division principle and the reason combinations exist.

Example 5 (choices that lean on earlier ones). Varun picks 2 different bagel types (order does not matter). For each type he picked, Varun puts on one of the 2 spreads. Kapil must then use the other spread on that same type. How many ways can this happen?

Step 1: Varun picks 2 types out of the 4. That is \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) ways. (We learn combinations next. For now, just pick two types from Plain, Sesame, Everything, and Poppy.)

Step 2: Take Varun's first type. He picks 1 of the 2 spreads, so 2 ways. Kapil is then forced to use the leftover spread, so 1 way. The second type works the same way. That gives \(2 \times 1 \times 2 \times 1 = 4\) spread setups.

Total: \(6 \times 4 = 24\) ways.

Aha: Kapil's choice depends on what Varun did. You can still multiply. "Independent" here means the number of options stays the same. It does not mean the choices are unrelated. Varun always has 2 spread options and Kapil always has 1.

Example 6 (an overlapping "or"). How many breakfasts (bagel type + spread) use either a double-quantity type (Plain or Sesame) or the onion & chives spread? A breakfast that is both a double-quantity type and onion & chives still counts, but only one time.

Two overlapping groups. Let \(A\) = breakfasts with a double-quantity type: \(2\text{ types} \times 2\text{ spreads} = 4\). Let \(B\) = breakfasts with the onion & chives spread: \(4\text{ types} \times 1\text{ spread} = 4\). A breakfast can be in both groups. That happens when it is a double-quantity type and has onion & chives. So the groups overlap: \(|A \cap B| = 2 \times 1 = 2\). If you just add \(|A| + |B|\), you count those 2 overlap breakfasts twice. So subtract them back one time: \[ |A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B| = 4 + 4 - 2 = 6. \]

Cross-check with disjoint cases. You can also split the answer into pieces that do not overlap, then just add them. No correction is needed. The pieces are: double-quantity with plain spread \((2)\), double-quantity with onion & chives \((2)\), and triple-quantity with onion & chives \((2)\). That gives \(2 + 2 + 2 = 6\). Splitting into disjoint cases avoids the double-count from the start.

Aha: Plain addition works only for disjoint cases. When the two "or" groups can overlap, add them and subtract the overlap one time (a preview of Inclusion-Exclusion). Or slice the problem into disjoint cases so there is no overlap to fix.

Two contest-level examples (AMC-10)

The bagel examples above are small enough to draw and check by hand. Contest problems use the same two rules, multiply and add, but at a size where you cannot list every case. Here are two digit-counting problems at roughly AMC-10 difficulty. Each one needs the multiplication principle inside a case and the addition principle to combine the cases, and each hides the same trap: the leading digit of a number cannot be 0, which quietly changes the count.

Example 7 (AMC-10 level). How many three-digit numbers (100 through 999) have exactly one digit equal to 5?

Read the English first. "Exactly one digit equal to 5" means one of the three digits is a 5 and the other two are anything except 5. A three-digit number has a hundreds digit (1 through 9, never 0), a tens digit (0 through 9), and a units digit (0 through 9). The single 5 can sit in any one of the three places, and those three situations cannot happen at the same time. That is a natural split into disjoint cases, so count each place separately and add.

  • The 5 is the hundreds digit. The hundreds place is fixed at 5, so 1 way. The tens digit is anything but 5, so 9 choices. The units digit is anything but 5, so 9 choices. That gives \(1 \times 9 \times 9 = 81\).
  • The 5 is the tens digit. The tens place is fixed at 5. The hundreds digit must be 1 through 9 and not 5, so 8 choices. The units digit is anything but 5, so 9 choices. That gives \(8 \times 1 \times 9 = 72\).
  • The 5 is the units digit. The units place is fixed at 5. The hundreds digit is 1 through 9 and not 5, so 8 choices. The tens digit is anything but 5, so 9 choices. That gives \(8 \times 9 \times 1 = 72\).

The three cases are disjoint (the lone 5 lives in exactly one place) and together they cover every number with exactly one 5, so add: \[ 81 + 72 + 72 = 225. \]

Cross-check a different way. Count the three-digit numbers with no 5 at all: the hundreds digit is 1 through 9 except 5 (8 choices), the tens is 0 through 9 except 5 (9 choices), the units the same (9 choices), so \(8 \times 9 \times 9 = 648\). There are 900 three-digit numbers in all, so \(900 - 648 = 252\) have at least one 5. Among those, the numbers with two 5s number 26 and the single number 555 has three, so exactly one 5 is \(252 - 26 - 1 = 225\). The two methods agree.

Aha: the multiplication principle counts inside one case, and the addition principle glues the cases together. The hundreds place behaves differently from the other two because it cannot be 0. That is exactly why the "5 in the hundreds" case gives 81 while the other two give 72. Whenever a digit problem touches the leading place, give it its own care: the "no leading zero" rule silently changes the count. Casing on WHERE a special digit sits is a move you will use again in Chapter 6: Casework.

Example 8 (AMC-10 level). How many four-digit numbers (1000 through 9999) are even and have four different digits?

Read the English first. "Even" means the units digit is one of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. "Four different digits" means no digit repeats. A four-digit number also has a thousands digit that cannot be 0. The trap is that two of the slots have special rules, the units must be even and the thousands cannot be 0, and both rules fight over the single digit 0. So split on the units digit: is it 0, or one of 2, 4, 6, 8? Those two cases cannot overlap, and together they cover every even number, so count each and add. Inside a case, fill one place at a time and subtract the digits already used.

Case 1: the units digit is 0. Now 0 is used up, so the thousands digit can be any of 1 through 9 (9 choices), the hundreds digit any remaining digit (8 choices), and the tens digit any remaining (7 choices). The units digit is fixed at 0. \[ 9 \times 8 \times 7 \times 1 = 504. \]

Case 2: the units digit is 2, 4, 6, or 8. Pick the units digit first: 4 choices. The thousands digit must be 1 through 9 and different from that units digit; since the units digit is a nonzero even number, it removes one option, leaving 8 choices. The hundreds digit can be any of the 10 digits except the two already used, so 8 choices. The tens digit is any of the remaining 7. \[ 4 \times 8 \times 8 \times 7 = 1792. \]

The two cases are disjoint and together cover every even four-digit number with distinct digits, so add: \[ 504 + 1792 = 2296. \]

Cross-check a different way. Count the four-digit numbers with all different digits that are odd instead. The units digit is one of 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 (5 choices, all nonzero), the thousands digit is 1 through 9 and different from it (8 choices), the hundreds any of the remaining 8, the tens any of the remaining 7: \(5 \times 8 \times 8 \times 7 = 2240\). The total number of four-digit numbers with all different digits is \(9 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 4536\). So the even ones number \(4536 - 2240 = 2296\), which matches.

Aha: the two special slots (units must be even, thousands cannot be 0) both want the digit 0, so casing on the units digit pulls them apart. The rule of thumb: fill the most-restricted places first, then the free ones, always subtracting the digits already used. Multiplication does the filling inside a case; addition combines the cases. This "deal with the constraint first" habit is the same one from practice problem P6 below and from restricted seating in Permutations.
🎯 The capstone we're building toward: In how many ways can we hand out the 10 bagels to the 4 kids, then put one of 2 spreads on each bagel? That needs one more tool: Stars & Bars (distribute identical bagels of each type among the kids), combined with the multiplication principle (across types, and for the spreads). We'll finish it on the Stars & Bars page. Come back and see how the whole map fits together.
Common pitfalls:
  • Mixing up AND/OR: Multiplying disjoint alternatives (should add) or adding independent steps (should multiply). Ask: "Do I make both choices (AND → ×) or pick between alternatives (OR → +)?"
  • Forgetting shrinking options: When "different / no repeats" appears, later steps have fewer options. \(4 \times 4 \times 4\) (with repeats) ≠ \(4 \times 3 \times 2\) (no repeats).
  • Overcounting overlaps: Adding cases that aren't disjoint counts the overlap twice. Sketch a Venn diagram if unsure.
  • Order confusion: Does the sequence matter? "Pick 2 bagels" might mean ordered (AB ≠ BA, use multiplication) or unordered (AB = BA, use combinations). Context tells you which.

Common variations & subtle points

  • With vs without replacement: "Pick 3 bagels from the 10" could mean (a) with replacement (pick, put back, pick again, same bagel can appear multiple times): \(10 \times 10 \times 10 = 10^3\) ordered outcomes; or (b) without replacement (once picked, it's gone): \(10 \times 9 \times 8\). The phrase "different bagels" signals without replacement.
  • Ordered vs unordered: "Assign 3 bagels to 3 kids" (who gets which) is ordered (multiplication principle, \(10 \times 9 \times 8\) if all different). "Choose 3 bagels to toast" (just which ones, not who gets them) is unordered (combinations, \(\binom{10}{3}\)). Context matters!
  • At-least / at-most: "At least one Everything bagel in your 3 picks" is easier via complement: (total ways) minus (ways with zero Everything) = \(10^3 - 7^3 = 1000 - 343 = 657\) if picking with replacement from the 10 bagels (3 are Everything, 7 aren't).
  • Counting problems that hide a "what happened first": Sometimes a counting problem is really about conditional probability. Take "if Varun picked an Everything bagel, how many ways can the other kids pick?" The count depends on what happened first.

Connections

  • → Permutations: the multiplication principle with shrinking options, \(n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\) (Example 2).
  • → Combinations & Overcounting: when order shouldn't matter, count ordered then divide (Example 4's move).
  • → Stars & Bars: the capstone bagel-distribution question lives here.
  • → Inclusion-Exclusion: the addition principle when cases overlap. Add, then subtract the double-counted part.
  • → Chapter 6: Casework: the addition principle used with discipline. Split a hard count into disjoint, exhaustive cases, count each with the multiplication principle, and add (Examples 7 and 8). The cross-checks there lean on Chapter 5: Complementary Counting (count the total minus the unwanted part).
  • → Probability: probability = (favorable count) ÷ (total count); both counts come from these two rules.
  • ↔ Algebra: exponents and factorials are really just counting. \(2^{10}\) counts the ways to put one of the 2 spreads on each of 10 bagels; \(n!\) counts orderings. This is the bridge combinatorics ↔ algebra.

★ Landmark it points toward

Generating functions: the "grown-up" multiplication principle: encode each choice as a polynomial and multiply the polynomials so the product's coefficients count the combined choices. (Just name it now.)

Practice

P1. Each of the 4 kids independently picks a bagel type (4, repeats allowed) and a spread (2). How many outcomes for the whole group?

AnswerEach kid: \(4\times 2 = 8\). Four independent kids: \(8^4 = 4096\).

P2. Of the 8 possible breakfasts (type × spread), how many are either an Everything bagel or have plain spread?

AnswerEverything: 2 (either spread); plain spread: 4 (one per type); both (Everything + plain): 1. These overlap, so \(2+4-1=5\). A first taste of Inclusion-Exclusion.

Why subtract the 1: the "or" here lets a breakfast satisfy both conditions (an Everything bagel with plain spread), and that breakfast sits in both piles. So adding the piles counts it twice. Subtracting the single overlap fixes the double-count.

Pattern (union of overlapping sets): \(|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|\). Plain addition only works when the cases cannot overlap; the moment "or" lets something qualify twice, add the pieces then subtract the shared part. Scale this up to three or more overlapping sets and it becomes Inclusion-Exclusion.

P3. In how many orders can the 4 kids line up to collect their bagels?

Answer\(4! = 24\). A pure permutation of the kids.

P4. We make 3 sandwiches for lunch using our bagels. The first sandwich gets a Plain or Sesame bagel, the second gets an Everything or Poppy, and the third gets any of the 4 types. Each sandwich gets any of the 2 spreads. How many ways to make the 3 sandwiches?

AnswerSandwich 1: \(2 \times 2 = 4\) (2 type choices, 2 spreads). Sandwich 2: \(2 \times 2 = 4\). Sandwich 3: \(4 \times 2 = 8\). Total: \(4 \times 4 \times 8 = 128\).

P5. Varun and Kapil each pick a different bagel type (no repeats between them), and Shlok picks a different type from both of theirs. How many ways?

AnswerVarun: 4 choices. Kapil: 3 remaining choices (different from Varun). Shlok: 2 remaining choices (different from both). Total: \(4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24\).

P6 (challenge). We give each of the 4 kids exactly one bagel from our stash of 10. Kapil is allergic to sesame, so he can't get a Sesame bagel. The other kids can get any type. In how many ways can we choose which specific kid gets which specific bagel (treating same-type bagels as distinguishable for now, say they're numbered 1 to 10)?

AnswerThere are 10 bagels total. Kapil can receive any of the 8 non-Sesame bagels (2 Plain + 3 Everything + 3 Poppy = 8). After Kapil picks, 9 bagels remain and the other 3 kids pick in sequence: \(9 \times 8 \times 7\) ways. Total: \(8 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 4032\).

Why handle Kapil first: the restriction lives on Kapil, so pin down the hard choice while it is still simple. He has \(8\) legal bagels. Once he is served, nobody else has a restriction, so the rest is an ordinary shrinking count \(9 \times 8 \times 7\). If you seated the unrestricted kids first, you would have to stop and ask "is a Sesame still left for Kapil?", turning one clean count into messy cases.

Pattern (deal with the constraint first): when one person or slot is special, assign it before the free ones. This "hardest choice first" habit keeps the later steps unconstrained, and it is the same idea as the restricted-seating problems in Permutations.

P7. How many 3-digit numbers can you form where the hundreds digit is either 1, 2, or 3; the tens digit is either 0 or 5; and the units digit is any digit 0 to 9?

AnswerHundreds: 3 choices (1, 2, or 3). Tens: 2 choices (0 or 5). Units: 10 choices. Total: \(3 \times 2 \times 10 = 60\).
