The average was \(24/4 = 6\), \(84/6 = 14\), \(156/12 = 13\), and \(240/24 = 10\), and each one was confirmed by an independent by-hand count. Naive division, \(N\) arrangements over \(|G|\) moves, gave a non-integer every time it would have been wrong. That is the tell: when division fails, averaging still works. Before we state the rule, three plain names for what we kept using.

  • A group of symmetries \(G\). A symmetry is an allowed move you treat as not changing the object. The full set of them is the group \(G\), and \(|G|\) is how many there are. Two facts make a set of moves a group, and both held above: doing one move then another is again an allowed move, and every move can be undone. Spins only give the cyclic group \(C_n\), with \(|G| = n\). Spins and flips together give the dihedral group \(D_n\), with \(|G| = 2n\).
  • An orbit. Start from one arrangement and apply every move; the arrangements you reach form its orbit, which is exactly one group of "these all count as the same." The number of distinct arrangements is the number of orbits. This is what we counted.
  • The fixed count \(\text{Fix}(g)\). For a move \(g\), \(\text{Fix}(g)\) is the number of arrangements it leaves looking identical. This is the "how many unchanged" number we computed for each move.

Burnside's lemma

The rule the three cases discovered has a name: Burnside's lemma. It says the number of distinct arrangements (the number of orbits) is the average of \(\text{Fix}(g)\) over the whole group: \[ \text{number of distinct arrangements} = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \text{Fix}(g). \] In words: for each symmetry, count how many arrangements it leaves unchanged, add those counts, and divide by the number of symmetries. Plain division \(N/|G|\) from Chapter 4: Overcounting / Division Principle is just the special case where the identity is the only move that fixes anything, so every orbit is full size \(|G|\) and the average collapses to \(N/|G|\).

Why the average works. Make a big table with one row per symmetry and one column per arrangement, and put a check in a cell when that symmetry leaves that arrangement unchanged. Count the checks two ways.

  • By rows: row \(g\) has \(\text{Fix}(g)\) checks, so the table holds \(\sum_{g} \text{Fix}(g)\) checks in total.
  • By columns: a given arrangement collects a check from every symmetry that leaves it unchanged. Here is the key fact, the orbit-stabilizer relationship: if an arrangement sits in an orbit of \(s\) look-alikes, then exactly \(|G|/s\) symmetries leave it unchanged. So each of the \(s\) arrangements in that orbit contributes \(|G|/s\) checks, and the whole orbit contributes \(s \cdot |G|/s = |G|\) checks. Every orbit puts exactly \(|G|\) checks in the table, no matter its size.

If there are \(N\) orbits, the column count is \(N \cdot |G|\). Setting the two counts equal, \(\sum_{g} \text{Fix}(g) = N \cdot |G|\), so \[ N = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\text{Fix}(g). \] The unequal orbit sizes are exactly what division could not handle and what this averaging absorbs cleanly.

Aha: plain division asks "how many arrangements, and how many times did I count each?" Burnside asks an easier question of each move: "how many arrangements do you leave untouched?" The average of those answers is the orbit count, and it never assumes the groups are equal.

Pólya's enumeration theorem (the generalization)

Burnside answers "how many distinct arrangements?" Pólya's enumeration theorem answers the richer question "how many distinct arrangements use exactly this many of each color?" all at once, by attaching a variable to each color. It is the professional tool for counting up to symmetry, and the necklace and cube counts above are its simplest cases. We show the idea, not the full machinery.

The cycle index of a group

Every move \(g\) breaks the positions into loops (cycles). Record a move by writing \(a_1\) for each fixed point, \(a_2\) for each 2-cycle, \(a_3\) for each 3-cycle, and so on. The cycle index \(Z(G)\) is the average of these products over the whole group. For the spins of a 6-bead necklace, group the spins by \(\gcd(j,6)\) exactly as in Case 2:

\[ Z(C_6) = \frac{1}{6}\Big(a_1^{6} + a_2^{3} + 2\,a_3^{2} + 2\,a_6\Big). \]

Here \(a_1^6\) is the identity (six fixed points), \(a_2^3\) is the spin by 3 (three 2-cycles), the two \(a_3^2\) terms are the spins by 2 and 4 (two 3-cycles each), and the two \(a_6\) terms are the spins by 1 and 5 (one 6-cycle each).

Turning the cycle index into a count

Just the total. To count all necklaces in \(k\) colors, set every \(a_i = k\) (each cycle is one free choice of \(k\) colors): \[ Z(C_6)\big|_{a_i = k} = \frac{k^6 + k^3 + 2k^2 + 2k}{6}. \] For \(k = 2\) this is \(\frac{64 + 8 + 8 + 4}{6} = \frac{84}{6} = 14\), the Case 2 answer. Regrouping the same terms by the divisors of 6 gives the classic necklace formula \[ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{d \mid n} \varphi(d)\, k^{\,n/d}, \] where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function (it counts how many spins share each cycle structure). This is exactly the formula named at the end of Chapter 4.

Tracking each color (the real power). Instead of \(a_i = k\), substitute \(a_i = b^i + w^i\) for two colors black and white. Now the answer is a polynomial in \(b\) and \(w\), and the coefficient of \(b^r w^{6-r}\) is the number of distinct necklaces with exactly \(r\) black beads. Working it out for \(C_6\) gives \[ b^6 + b^5 w + 3b^4 w^2 + 4b^3 w^3 + 3b^2 w^4 + b\,w^5 + w^6, \] so the necklaces split as \(1, 1, 3, 4, 3, 1, 1\) by number of black beads, which is the by-hand cross-check from Case 2, now produced automatically. That refinement, getting the full breakdown by color usage from one polynomial, is what Pólya's theorem adds on top of Burnside.

Aha: Burnside is Pólya with the colors "switched off" (every \(a_i\) set to the plain color count \(k\)). Keep the variables on, and the same average delivers the entire distribution by color, not just the grand total. The cycle index is the one object that stores everything the group's symmetry does to the count.

Common pitfalls

Do not just divide, and do not just halve. Plain division \(N/|G|\) is right only when the identity is the sole move that leaves anything unchanged (all orbits full size). The moment a rotation or a flip can leave an arrangement looking the same, some orbits shrink, and both "divide by \(|G|\)" and "take the rotation answer and halve for flips" undercount. Use the full Burnside average. A quick tell: if \(N/|G|\) is not a whole number, division was never valid to begin with.
Count cycles correctly, and use the right group. The fixed count of a move is \(k^{(\text{number of cycles})}\), so the whole problem hinges on getting each move's cycle structure right. Two classic slips: forgetting that a reflection of an even necklace comes in two axis types (through beads vs through gaps) that leave different amounts unchanged, and using \(C_n\) (rotations only) when the object can also be flipped, which needs \(D_n\). Always ask first: exactly which moves count as "the same," and list every one.

Connections

  • ← Chapter 4: Overcounting / Division Principle: the home of the division shortcut. Plain division is the special case here where every orbit is full size; this chapter is what to do when the orbits are unequal and division fails. The bracelet-with-flips example flagged there as needing this method is worked in full above.
  • ← Chapter 2: Permutations: every symmetry is a permutation of the positions, and its cycle structure is what drives the fixed count. Reading a move as "which positions cycle into which" is the core skill.
  • ↔ Chapter 1: Counting Principles: a move leaves \(k^{(\text{cycles})}\) colorings unchanged by the multiplication principle, one independent color choice per cycle.
  • ↔ Chapter 3: Combinations: the by-color cross-checks (necklaces or cube faces sorted by how many are one color) are combinations first, then corrected for symmetry, which is precisely what Pólya's color-tracking does in one step.
  • ↔ Group theory (Algebra): \(C_n\) and \(D_n\) and the cube's rotation group are the first real groups most students meet, and "number of orbits" is the quantity Burnside computes. This chapter is a doorway into abstract algebra.
  • ↔ Chemistry and graph theory: counting distinct molecules (atoms placed on a symmetric skeleton) and distinct graphs on labeled-then-unlabeled vertices are the headline applications of Pólya's theorem.

★ Landmarks it points toward

Pólya's enumeration theorem in full, via the cycle index. The general statement builds the cycle index of any symmetry group and substitutes a "figure-counting series" for the colors, producing generating functions that count colorings by exact color content. It powers the enumeration of chemical isomers, unlabeled graphs and trees, and switching networks. (Named here, taught in a course on combinatorial enumeration or group theory, one level above Burnside.)

The orbit-stabilizer theorem. The group-theory identity that proves Burnside's lemma: the size of an orbit times the number of moves that fix any one of its members equals \(|G|\). It is the exact statement of "small orbits come from extra symmetry," and it is the key fact used in the proof above.

Practice

P1. How many distinct necklaces of 4 beads in 2 colors are there under rotation only (spins, no flips)?

AnswerGroup \(C_4\). Fixed counts: \(2^4=16\) (identity), \(2\) (spin 1), \(2^2=4\) (spin 2), \(2\) (spin 3). Average \(\frac{16+2+4+2}{4} = \frac{24}{4} = 6\). Same number as the square-corner count that opened the chapter, since a 4-bead loop and a square's corners have the same rotation group.

P2. How many distinct necklaces of 5 beads in 2 colors are there under rotation only?

AnswerGroup \(C_5\). Since 5 is prime, every non-identity spin is a single 5-cycle fixing only the all-one-color loops. Fixed counts: \(2^5=32\) (identity) and \(2^1=2\) for each of the 4 other spins. Average \(\frac{32 + 4\cdot 2}{5} = \frac{40}{5} = 8\).

P3. Color the 3 corners of an equilateral triangle with 2 colors, where turning the triangle counts as the same. How many distinct colorings?

AnswerGroup \(C_3\) (rotations by 0, 120, 240). Fixed: \(2^3=8\) (identity), \(2^1=2\), \(2^1=2\). Average \(\frac{8+2+2}{3} = \frac{12}{3} = 4\).

P4 (EXPAND). How many distinct bracelets of 5 beads in 2 colors are there under rotation and reflection?

AnswerGroup \(D_5\), \(|G| = 10\). The 5 rotations give \(32 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 40\) (from P2). For odd \(n\) every reflection axis passes through one bead and the midpoint of the opposite gap, so each flip fixes that 1 bead and swaps the other 4 in 2 pairs: \(1 + 2 = 3\) cycles, \(\text{Fix} = 2^3 = 8\). Five reflections give \(5 \times 8 = 40\). Average \(\frac{40 + 40}{10} = \frac{80}{10} = 8\).

Why it works: unlike the 6-bead case, an odd necklace has only one reflection type, because a mirror line through one bead must miss all the others in pairs. That single type makes the reflection bookkeeping short. Here the bracelet count (8) happens to equal the necklace count (also 8 for 5 beads), because for these small numbers every 5-bead necklace already equals its own mirror image, so the flips merge nothing.

Pattern (odd vs even reflection axes): for a loop of \(n\) beads, count reflections by axis type before averaging. Odd \(n\): all \(n\) axes are the same, each fixing 1 bead and \((n-1)/2\) pairs. Even \(n\): \(n/2\) axes run through 2 beads and \(n/2\) run through 2 gaps, and the two types fix different amounts. Get this split right and the dihedral average falls out.

P5 (EXPAND). How many distinct necklaces of 6 beads in 3 colors are there under rotation only?

AnswerGroup \(C_6\), same cycle structure as Case 2 but with \(k = 3\). Using \(\text{Fix} = 3^{\gcd(j,6)}\): \(3^6=729\) (j=0), \(3\) (j=1), \(3^2=9\) (j=2), \(3^3=27\) (j=3), \(9\) (j=4), \(3\) (j=5). Average \(\frac{729 + 3 + 9 + 27 + 9 + 3}{6} = \frac{780}{6} = 130\).

Why it works: the group and its cycle counts do not depend on the number of colors, so the exact same six cycle counts \((6,1,2,3,2,1)\) get reused with a base of 3 instead of 2. This is the divisor formula \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)\,k^{n/d}\) with \(n = 6\), \(k = 3\): \(\frac{1}{6}(\varphi(1)3^6 + \varphi(2)3^3 + \varphi(3)3^2 + \varphi(6)3^1) = \frac{729 + 27 + 2\cdot 9 + 2\cdot 3}{6} = 130\).

Pattern (change the colors, reuse the cycle counts): once you have a group's cycle structure, counting in a new number of colors is just a new base in \(k^{(\text{cycles})}\). Compute the cycle counts once, then plug in any \(k\). The cycle index makes this a single substitution.

P6 (EXPAND, AMC-10 level). Paint the 6 faces of a cube in 3 colors (colors may repeat, and any color usage is allowed). Two paintings are the same if one can be turned into the other. How many distinct paintings?

AnswerReuse the cube's 5 rotation families and their face-cycle counts \((6,3,4,2,3)\) from Case 3, now with \(k = 3\): \[ \frac{1\cdot 3^6 + 6\cdot 3^3 + 3\cdot 3^4 + 8\cdot 3^2 + 6\cdot 3^3}{24} = \frac{729 + 162 + 243 + 72 + 162}{24} = \frac{1368}{24} = 57. \]

Why it works: the cube's rotation group and its face-cycle structure are fixed facts about the cube, independent of how many paint colors you own. So the whole Case 3 table carries over unchanged, and only the base of the powers changes from 2 to 3. This is why setting up the cycle counts once pays off: 2 colors gives 10, 3 colors gives 57, and \(k\) colors gives \(\frac{k^6 + 3k^4 + 12k^3 + 8k^2}{24}\) from the same five terms.

Pattern (symmetric solids are a fixed cycle table): for any Platonic solid, work out once how each rotation family cycles the faces (or vertices, or edges), then Burnside in \(k\) colors is one weighted average. The hard part is the geometry table, done a single time; the counting is then mechanical for any number of colors.

P7 (EXPAND, hard). How many distinct bracelets of 6 beads in 3 colors are there under rotation and reflection?

AnswerGroup \(D_6\), \(|G| = 12\), combining the P5 rotations with the two reflection types from Case 2, all at \(k = 3\).
  • 6 rotations: \(729 + 3 + 9 + 27 + 9 + 3 = 780\) (from P5).
  • 3 bead-axis flips (2 fixed beads + 2 pairs = 4 cycles): \(3 \times 3^4 = 3 \times 81 = 243\).
  • 3 gap-axis flips (3 pairs = 3 cycles): \(3 \times 3^3 = 3 \times 27 = 81\).
Average \(\frac{780 + 243 + 81}{12} = \frac{1104}{12} = 92\).

Why it works: this problem stacks everything in the chapter. The rotation part is the necklace count P5, the reflection part splits into the two axis types of an even loop (Case 2), and the color base is 3 (P5, P6). Each piece is a small Burnside sub-count; assemble them and divide by \(|G| = 12\). As a sanity check, the answer 92 is less than the 130 rotation-only necklaces, which is right because adding flips can only merge orbits, never create them.

Pattern (build a big Burnside from known pieces): for a large symmetry group, do not compute every move from scratch. Reuse the rotation sub-count you already have, add the reflection families by axis type, keep the color base consistent, then average over the full group. The method scales because each family contributes one clean term.

Teaching notes

Opener (discover before naming): do the square first, cold. Ask "color 4 corners in 2 colors, turns count as the same, how many truly different colorings?" Let them list and reach 6 by hand. Then show the bookkeeping that also gives 6: for each of the 4 turns, count how many colorings it leaves unchanged (16, 2, 4, 2), and average. Do not say "Burnside" yet. The point is that the average, not the division \(16/4\), is what matched their hand count.

Board moves: the reusable ritual is three columns, "move, its cycles, \(k^{\text{cycles}}\)," then average. Run the necklace this way (answer 14), stressing that a spin by \(j\) makes \(\gcd(j,6)\) cycles. Then add flips for the bracelet (answer 13) to introduce reflections and the two axis types of an even loop. Save the cube (answer 10) for when the ritual is automatic, since the payoff is learning to read a 3D rotation as a face permutation.

Name it only after the pattern: once all three counts are on the board, write the average formula and call it Burnside's lemma, then run the row-and-column "why it works" argument so the average is not a mystery. Point back to Chapter 4: Overcounting / Division Principle: plain division is the special case where only the identity fixes anything.

The two hard ones: the bracelet under \(D_6\) is where students want to just halve 14 to get 7; make them see the mirror-symmetric necklaces are not merged, so halving undercounts, and the honest count is 13. The cube faces is the classic contest problem; build the 5-family table slowly and check that \(1+6+3+8+6 = 24\) before averaging. Both have a by-hand cross-check (sort by color count), so do the cross-check out loud to cement trust.

What to name: "group," "cyclic group \(C_n\)," "dihedral group \(D_n\)," "orbit" (a bin of same-looking arrangements), "\(\text{Fix}(g)\)," and lightly "cycle index." Keep the language plain: an orbit is "everything that counts as the same thing," a fixed coloring is "one the move leaves looking identical."

Common stumble: miscounting a move's cycles, especially reflections of an even necklace (two axis types) and cube corner-turns (two 3-cycles, not something else). Have them physically turn a die or a drawn hexagon and trace where each face or bead goes. Also drill the reflex "which moves count as the same?" so they pick \(C_n\) vs \(D_n\) correctly before computing.

Pacing and depth: the three discovery counts plus naming Burnside is a full, satisfying lesson. Treat the Pólya section as the reach goal: show the cycle index of \(C_6\) and the two substitutions (all \(a_i = k\) for the total, \(a_i = b^i + w^i\) for the color breakdown), then name the general theorem as a landmark. The color-tracking polynomial reproducing \(1,1,3,4,3,1,1\) is the moment to reveal why anyone bothers with the cycle index.

Glossary

Quick definitions, grouped by layer of the concept map.

Foundation (the spine)

Addition Principle
If the possibilities split into cases that do not overlap, the total is the sum of the case counts. Reach for it whenever the word "or" separates mutually-exclusive options.
Multiplication Principle (Fundamental Counting Principle)
If a process is a sequence of independent steps offering \(n_1, n_2, \dots\) choices, the number of outcomes is the product \(n_1 \cdot n_2 \cdots\). "And" between independent choices means multiply.
Factorial \(n!\)
The product \(n\cdot(n-1)\cdots 2\cdot 1\) . It is the number of ways to order \(n\) distinct objects in a row. By convention \(0! = 1\).
Permutation \(P(n,k)\)
The number of ORDERED arrangements of \(k\) items chosen from \(n\): \(P(n,k)=n!/(n-k)! = n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)\). Order matters (gold vs. silver medal are different).
Combination \(C(n,k)\)
The number of UNORDERED selections of \(k\) items from \(n\): \(C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n-k)!)\). It is a permutation divided by \(k!\), because the \(k\) chosen items can be ordered \(k!\) ways we don't want to distinguish.
Overcounting / Division Principle
Count arrangements as if order or symmetry matters, then divide by how many of them represent the same thing. This is why \(C(n,k)=P(n,k)/k!\) and why round-table seatings divide by the number of rotations.
Multiset permutation
Arrangements of \(n\) objects when some are identical: \(n!/(n_1!\,n_2!\cdots)\). Example: lining up the 10 bagels (2, 2, 3, 3 of each type) gives \(10!/(2!\,2!\,3!\,3!)=25{,}200\).

Core techniques

Complementary Counting
Instead of counting what you want, count everything and subtract what you don't: good = all minus bad. Ideal when the condition is "at least one," which is awkward to count head-on.
Casework
Break a problem into disjoint, exhaustive cases, count each separately, and add. The skill is choosing cases that are clean and never overlap.
Stars & Bars
The number of ways to place \(n\) IDENTICAL items into \(k\) DISTINCT boxes (empties allowed) is \(C(n+k-1,\,k-1)\) . Equivalently, it is the number of non-negative integer solutions of \(x_1+\cdots+x_k=n\).
Pigeonhole Principle
If more than \(m\) items go into \(m\) boxes, some box holds at least two; more generally some box holds at least \(\lceil n/m\rceil\). It proves a collision must exist without finding it.
Inclusion-Exclusion (PIE)
To count a union of overlapping sets, add the individual sizes, subtract the pairwise overlaps, add back the triple overlaps, and so on with alternating signs. This fixes the double-counting that plain addition causes.
Bijection
A one-to-one, onto pairing between two sets; if one exists, the sets are exactly the same size. Combinatorics uses it to recount a hard set as an easy one (e.g. subsets ↔ binary strings).
Recursion / Recurrence
Expressing the count for size \(n\) in terms of smaller sizes, e.g. \(f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n-2)\). You "condition" on a first or last choice to shrink the problem.
Symmetry argument
When two outcomes are interchangeable, they occur equally often. So you can count one and multiply, or split a total in half (e.g. Varun is left of Kapil in exactly half of all line-ups).

Objects & sequences

Binomial Coefficient \(C(n,k)\)
The number of \(k\)-element subsets of an \(n\)-set; the entries of Pascal's triangle; the coefficients in \((x+y)^n\). Read aloud as "n choose k."
Pascal's Triangle
A triangular array where each entry is the sum of the two above it, \(C(n,k)=C(n-1,k-1)+C(n-1,k)\). Row \(n\) lists \(C(n,0),\dots,C(n,n)\) and sums to \(2^n\).
Binomial Theorem
\((x+y)^n=\sum_k C(n,k)\,x^{n-k}y^k\). The bridge from counting to algebra: each coefficient literally counts the ways to choose that many \(x\)'s.
Hockey Stick Identity
Summing a diagonal of Pascal's triangle gives the entry just past its end: \(C(r,r)+C(r{+}1,r)+\cdots+C(n,r)=C(n{+}1,r{+}1)\).
Vandermonde's Identity
\(\sum_k C(m,k)\,C(n,p-k)=C(m+n,p)\): choosing \(p\) items from two groups of sizes \(m\) and \(n\), split by how many come from each.
Lattice Path
A monotone path on a grid using unit Right/Up steps. The number from \((0,0)\) to \((m,n)\) is \(C(m+n,m)\), since a path is just a sequence of \(m\) R's and \(n\) U's.
Catalan Number
\(C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}\): 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, … It counts balanced parentheses, polygon triangulations, binary trees, and lattice paths that stay below the diagonal. It is the same structure in many forms.
Derangement
A permutation in which no element stays in its original position; \(D_n=n!\left(1-\tfrac1{1!}+\tfrac1{2!}-\cdots\right)\). For large \(n\), \(D_n/n!\to 1/e\approx 0.368\).
Fibonacci Numbers
\(1,1,2,3,5,8,\dots\) with \(f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n-2)\). They count \(1\times n\) tilings by squares and dominoes, and binary strings with no two adjacent 1s.
Probability
For equally-likely outcomes, \(P(\text{event})=\dfrac{\text{favorable}}{\text{total}}\). Because both parts are counts, every counting technique is also a probability technique.
Expected Value
The long-run average of a random quantity: \(E[X]=\sum(\text{value}\times\text{probability})\). It need not be a possible value itself (e.g. an average of 2.5 kids).
Linearity of Expectation
\(E[X_1+\cdots+X_n]=E[X_1]+\cdots+E[X_n]\) , ALWAYS, even when the parts are dependent. The trick: write a count as a sum of simple 0/1 indicator variables and add their easy expectations.

★ Landmarks (name-only, for later)

Generating functions
Encode a sequence \(a_0,a_1,\dots\) as the coefficients of a power series \(\sum a_k x^k\); multiplying series corresponds to combining independent choices, turning counting into algebra.
Burnside / Pólya
Count objects "up to symmetry" (rotations, reflections) by averaging, over all symmetries, the number of arrangements each one leaves unchanged.
Probabilistic method
Prove a structure exists by showing a randomly chosen one has the property with positive probability, without ever building it (Erdős's signature technique).
Ramsey theory
"Complete disorder is impossible": any large enough structure must contain an ordered sub-pattern. For example, any 6 people include 3 mutual friends or 3 mutual strangers.
Integer partitions
The ways to write \(n\) as a sum of positive integers ignoring order (\(4=3{+}1=2{+}2=\dots\)); visualized with Ferrers / Young diagrams.
Double counting
Count one quantity two different ways and set the results equal to prove an identity. For example, the handshake lemma (sum of degrees \(=2\times\) edges).
